content: In the healthcare system, an orphan patient refers to an individual who has become lost within the system or lacks a primary care provider to oversee their medical care. Typically, a primary care provider, such as a general practitioner or family doctor, manages a patient’s basic health needs and coordinates referrals to specialists for more complex medical issues. Patients without such a provider are often referred to as no-family-doctor patients. Healthcare professionals and insiders generally observe that orphan patients tend to receive suboptimal care compared to those who have a primary care provider acting as a gatekeeper to coordinate their medical needs. This lack of coordination can lead to fragmented and less effective care. Several factors contribute to the orphan patient issue in North America. These include challenges in maintaining an adequate supply of qualified healthcare practitioners, ensuring access to these providers where and when they are most needed, and addressing the demands of a growing and aging population. Additionally, the patient population is becoming sicker, with conditions such as diabetes and obesity being particularly prevalent. There is also a trend toward a more medicalized population, where expectations for medical care are higher, and more diseases are defined and treated. Furthermore, the complexity of treatments for well-known diseases has increased significantly; for example, the standard-of-care treatment for heart attacks is now far more labor-intensive than it was a decade ago. The orphan patient problem has only recently gained attention in the media, although the term was used as early as 1988 in a letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Addressing the orphan patient issue is inherently complex due to its multifactorial origins. Reducing the population size is not feasible, and increasing the number of physicians and healthcare providers is challenging due to the lengthy training periods required. Temporary solutions have focused on altering the way healthcare is delivered. These include: Expanding the use of alternative healthcare providers, such as nurse practitioners, hospitalists, and telehealth-based public information services. Leveraging technological tools, such as electronic medical records and telemedicine, to enhance the efficiency of existing healthcare providers. Implementing broader and more effective public health initiatives, such as smoking cessation programs and fitness campaigns, to reduce the overall burden of illness within communities. Political interventions, such as community smoking bans and seatbelt regulations, are additional measures that can alleviate the strain on the healthcare system. While these initiatives are sometimes spearheaded by medical professionals, they can also be implemented independently of their involvement.
